comments.text:
Here is the official comment from AMD…

“It’s correct that 14 Compute Unit (896 stream processors) and 16 Compute Unit (1024 stream processor) versions of the Radeon RX 560 are available. We introduced the 14CU version this summer to provide AIBs and the market with more RX 500 series options. It’s come to our attention that on certain AIB and etail websites there’s no clear delineation between the two variants. We’re taking immediate steps to remedy this: we’re working with all AIB and channel partners to make sure the product descriptions and names clarify the CU count, so that gamers and consumers know exactly what they’re buying. We apologize for the confusion this may have caused.”

So AMD has sort of taken the blame while also placing some on the AIB partners which is a bit weak. It’s not their job to name AMDs’ products for them. They were already selling Radeon RX 560 1024 SPU cards. All etail websites I spoke with didn’t even realize the change had occurred. Anyway hopefully this is sorted and made clear to consumers shortly.

+Hardware Unboxed : Let me explain.

It comes down to Three Things here:

1. Mindshare
2. Situation
3. Reputation

1. Mindshare.
NVIDIA has a Majority of Mindshare in the GPU Market. This is why People buy NVIDIA more often than AMD. However, NVIDIA has had a bigger history of controversial moves or decisions. Anyone remember the Defective 8800 GPUs? Geforce Driver 196.75? 267.52? The whole GTX 970 3.5GB Fiasco? No, All is Forgiven, Right?

Yet AMD gets the Reputation of "Bad Drivers", with no history so far, or actual evidence, of AMD Drivers actually killing any GPUs. (most of them are due to very stupid overclocking attempts, or potentially badly designed aftermarket cards, which XFX unfortunately does have a history of doing. The Same could be said for NVIDIA, but more on that below)

That comes back to what I said. The GTX 1070 ti, which is a Cut-Down GTX 1080 with the GDDR5 Memory of a 1070, comes out. It didn't need to be released, but it's available, and NVIDIA has the freedom to release such a GPU. But the ONLY reason the 1070 Ti exists is because of One GPU. AMD's RX Vega 56. And what does most Tech Reviewers do? "Say it's a good card, doesn't need to be there though.", and moves onto something else like it isn't a big deal. No Controversy, no Hooplah. (Even though people will be throwing $400+ at a GPU like this)

Yet AMD releases "Refreshes" of their GPUs (Like the R9 300 Series, or RX 500 Series), or Releases this Dinky little RX 560 EVO, which is a Cut-Down 560, or a 460 with Higher Clocks, and You, Paul's Hardware, and Bitwit and other Techsites want to Shit on AMD for such a Move. (Even though this is an Entry-Level Card, and the majority of Gamers usually target Mid-Range GPUs like the 1050 Ti, 1060, RX 570 and 580.)

This is how NVIDIA maintains such a high Mindshare. You don't show any neutrality to the companies, and make it sound like you favor one GPU Vendor over Another. That has to stop. If you want AMD to actually give a care about the Gaming Market, stop with the Mindshare games and double-standards.

2. Situation.
NVIDIA has much more profits than AMD Does. Therefore, they can afford to make a card like the GTX 1070 ti. AMD Cannot do such a move with their VEGA Cards, so they would have to do it to one of their Lower-Level Cards. The 560 Makes the most sense, as not much Gamers are buying it (Miners are though. Yes, Miners do also buy RX 560s) and since the RX 460 had 896 SPs, doing a 560 with 896 shouldn't be entirely bad. It's another option. You buy it or you don't. It's that Simple, just like the GTX 1070 and 1070 Ti. You didn't have to make such a big deal about it. But You did, and that's why I'm doing this. A Cut-Down 560 won't hurt AMD much in the financial sector, as it's an Entry-Level GPU, and there are many other GPUs out there that do better while costing more. However, with videos like this, it WILL harm AMD's Reputation, which I'm about to go into next.

3. Reputation.
NVIDIA can afford to make shoddy moves because of both factors I mentioned:
- They have the Majority Mindshare.
- They have Financial Stability.

AMD, However, Can't afford to take such a hit. That's why they swung for the fences with Ryzen and VEGA. It was All or nothing in 2017, and whatever happened, happened. Ryzen is a Huge Success, taking the Fight to Intel's CPU Market Once again, and VEGA, while not as successful, did make an impact in other markets, like Mining, Server, and Business. However, it was quickly tossed away by Gamers because of Unreasonable Expectations (aka those that thought it would compete with a 1080 ti). It could only compete with the GTX 1070 and 1080, and to gamers, that was not enough. As a result, VEGA is now swept under the rug and being stomped on, because it "Didn't deliver".

And Gamers Wonder why AMD isn't profiting much as a Business in 2017.......

All this Mindshare Favoring NVIDIA, allowing them to Prosper despite making Fatal Mistakes, and the public not bothering to care about them and go on their merry way while striking at AMD and butchering them with memes and other hateful stuff for almost the Exact Same mistakes.....

Stop showing Favoritism towards one company over another. Stop putting unreasonable expectations upon them. And Maybe, Just Maybe, AMD may surprise you.

comments.text:
That's not entirely true.

While a GT 1030 is a better buy than an RX 550, the RX 560 is a better buy than the GTX 1050 if you can find them within $20 of each other. The RX 560 has more VRAM to work with so that being the thing that holds back the card isn't a factor, and it's more suited for low-level APIs that have asynchronous compute enabled where it matches or outperforms even the 1050 Ti. For someone looking into buying such a budget GPU, I don't think they're going to be upgrading or buying new anytime soon, so the RX 560 is the better GPU to buy in the long term too.

The RX 570 and RX 580 aren't overpriced either because the RX 570 performs the same as a 3GB GTX 1060 for around the same price, the RX 580 currently outperforms the GTX 1060 6GB for around the same price too, and then with async compute they completely run away from their competition. Again, they're the better long term buy too.

With V56 vs GTX 1070, the V56 is a better performing card and with undervolting the reference cooler is usable, so at around MSRP it's the better buy. V64 needs aftermarket cooling but with it, it matches the GTX 1080 in Nvidia favoured titles and outperforms it in AMD favoured ones, and matches or outperforms the 1080 Ti with async compute, but again only if you can get a V64 with aftermarket cooling at around MSRP.

The best buy though is the V56 because with aftermarket cooling it can OC to near GTX 1080/V64 levels, or with a simple BIOS flash you can get a V56 to be on par with a V64. That's GTX 1080 performance for $100 less, or with async compute in consideration that's GTX 1080 Ti performance for $300 less.

With pricing and availability normalised, AMD's a strong competitor, especially for long term buyers.
